## What this session covers

The practical hour. Building lesson materials, differentiating them, and drafting feedback,
using AI for the parts of that work where it's reliable.

This is the session where Session 2's rule of thumb earns its keep. Nearly everything a
teacher wants help with here is a task where you already have the content and you need it
in a different shape: a rubric turned into student-facing language, a reading leveled for
three different groups, a worksheet built from a text you chose, feedback drafted against
work a student handed you. That's the side of the line where these tools are strong.

Bring something real to work on. A unit you're teaching this fall, a rubric you're not
happy with, a worksheet you'd like three versions of.

## Session outline

| Time | Segment |
|-----:|:--------|
| ~20 min | Planning and content creation, worked live |
| ~20 min | Differentiation and accessibility of materials |
| ~20 min | Feedback and grading, and where the limits are |

## Key points

- The tasks to hand over are the ones where you supply the substance and the tool
  changes the form. Ask where the content is coming from before you start.
- Differentiation is the strongest case in the whole workshop. Producing four versions of
  one reading at four levels is work teachers rarely have time to do by hand.
- Feedback drafting is real help. Grading isn't the same task, and the difference matters
  both practically and ethically.
- Whatever comes out has your name on it. Check it before it reaches a student.

## Planning and content creation

The reliable pattern is to give the tool your material and ask for a transformation of it.
Your unit objectives into a lesson sequence. Your chosen text into comprehension questions.
Your rubric into a checklist a fourteen-year-old can actually use. Your slide notes into a
handout.

The pattern that disappoints people is asking for the substance itself. "Write me a lesson
on the water cycle" produces something generic that you then rewrite, and the rewriting
costs about what writing it would have. "Here is my lesson on the water cycle, give me
three exit-ticket questions at different difficulty levels" produces something you can use.

Both look like reasonable requests. The second one works because you brought the content.

## Differentiation and accessibility

This is the strongest case in the workshop.

Producing the same reading at three levels, with a vocabulary list for the students who
need one, and a version that works with a screen reader, is valuable and
time-consuming. Most teachers do a fraction of it, not because they don't want to
but because the day doesn't contain the hours. This is transformation work of the
kind these tools handle well, and the source text is yours.

::: {.callout-caution}
## Two Cautions

Leveling a text changes it. Check that what came back still says what the original said,
particularly with anything technical or historical, because simplification quietly drops
qualifiers.

And a simplified text isn't the same thing as an accommodation. An IEP specifies
particular supports, and the fact that a tool can produce something adjacent to one doesn't
mean it satisfies it.
:::

## Feedback and grading

These are different tasks carrying different risks.

### Drafting feedback

This one's a good use. You've read the work, you know what you want to say, and you want it
written out warmly and at length for thirty students. Give the tool the student's work and
the points you want made, then edit what comes back. The judgment stayed with you.

### Assigning a grade

Different thing entirely. A score is a decision about a student, and these tools produce
plausible-looking scores with no consistency between runs and no defensible account of how
they got there. If a parent asks why their child got a 74, "the
model said so" isn't an answer any of us wants to give.

There's also a straightforward privacy question. Pasting student work into a commercial tool
sends it to a third party, and depending on your district and what's identifiable in it,
that might not be something you're permitted to do. Check before, not after.
